passages.title: Refuge in mankind's Lord from the whisperer
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah al-Nās is the Qurʼān's closing word: a prayer of refuge, placed on the tongue of every believer, from the most intimate enemy a human being has — the whisperer who works inside the chest. The six ayat form a single sentence with a single architecture: three names of Allah invoked (ayat 1–3), one evil named (ayat 4–5), and its two sources unmasked (ayah 6).

## Three names against one evil

The sūrah opens by piling up three divine attributes: *Rabb al-nās* — Lord of mankind; *Malik al-nās* — King of mankind; *Ilāh al-nās* — the Ilāh of mankind, the One truly worthy of worship. Ibn Kathir explains that these are lordship, sovereignty and divinity: Allah is the Lord of everything, the King of everything, and the Ilāh of everything — all things are created by Him, owned by Him, and subservient to Him. The one seeking protection is commanded to seek refuge with the One who possesses all three.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why each name is needed. *Rabb* means "one who nurtures" — but in Arabic the word can be attributed to others, as in *rabb al-dār* (landlord) or *rabb al-māl* (owner of wealth). Not every master is a king, so *Malik* is added; and not every king is worthy of worship, so *Ilāh* is added. Each attribute is itself a motive for protection: a master takes care of his servants, a king looks after his subjects, and that the One worshipped protects His worshipper is more obvious still. Only Allah holds all three attributes at once — so invoking them together is, in Maʿārif's words, the greatest protection, and such an invocation is readily acceptable.

Why "Lord of *mankind*" here, when the previous sūrah said "Lord of the *daybreak*"? Maʿārif (citing Mazhari from Baidawi) answers: al-Falaq sought protection from outward, bodily harms, which are not confined to human beings — animals suffer them too. But shaytanic instigation is restricted to man (with the jinn subjoined to him), so the Lord is here named specifically as mankind's Lord.

Notice also that *al-nās* is repeated five times. Maʿārif observes that the second and third verses could apparently have used a pronoun instead — *malikihim*, "their King" — but this is an occasion of supplication and praise, and in such speech repetition is employed by deliberate design: it adds force and clarity and creates a natural rhyme, rhythm and melodic sequence. Some scholars went further and read each occurrence as a stage of human life: the first refers to children (for *Rabb*, the Nurturer — children need nurturing most), the second to youth (for *Malik*, the King — kingship suits the vigour of youth), the third to old age (for *Ilāh* — the old cut themselves off from the world and look to Allah alone), the fourth to the righteous (for it is they whom the devil targets with his whispering), and the fifth to the mischief-makers from whose mischief protection is sought.

There is a deliberate imbalance here, and Maʿārif names it as the subtle difference between the two sūrahs of the Muʿawwadhatain (the two "refuge-seeking" sūrahs that close the Qurʼān). In al-Falaq, one attribute of Allah is invoked against many evils; in al-Nās, three attributes are invoked against a single evil — the whispering. This shows that the mischief of Shayṭān is the worst type of evil. Worldly calamities strike the body and one's earthly affairs, and a physical injury can be treated; but the Shayṭān lies hidden in ambush in every corner of a person's life, and his aim is the ruin of the Hereafter itself. Against such an enemy no remedy avails except the protection granted by Allah — hence three names are marshalled against him.

## The whisperer who withdraws

Ayah 4 names the enemy: *al-waswās al-khannās*, "the lurking whisperer". Both words repay attention.

*Waswās*, Maʿārif explains (citing Qurtubi), is originally an infinitive meaning *waswasah* — to whisper, to use breath instead of voice, saying something in a barely audible way. Applied to Shayṭān it is a hyperbole: he is *an embodiment of whisper*. His whispering means that he invites people to his obedience by casting a discourse into the heart in such a way that its content arrives but no voice is heard.

*Khannās* comes from *khanasa* — to sneak, recede, or withdraw furtively. The name captures his method. Saʿīd bin Jubayr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "The devil who is squatting (perched) upon the heart of the Son of Adam. So when he becomes absentminded and heedless he whispers. Then, when he remembers Allah he withdraws." Mujahid and Qatadah said the same. Al-Muʿtamir bin Sulaymān's father added that he blows into the heart of the Son of Adam when he is sad and when he is happy — but when man remembers Allah, he withdraws. And in another report from Ibn ʿAbbās: "He whispers, and then when he is obeyed, he withdraws." Maʿārif notes that this cycle continues persistently: whenever man becomes unmindful the Shayṭān returns; whenever he remembers Allah, he retreats.

Maʿārif also quotes a saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (transmitted by Abu Yaʿla on the authority of Anas, as quoted by Mazhari): Allah has built two houses in the heart of man — in one resides an angel, in the other the Shayṭān. The angel urges him to good works and the Shayṭān induces him to evil. When man remembers Allah, the Shayṭān withdraws; when he stops remembering, the Shayṭān perches on the heart and whispers into it.

Ibn Kathir grounds this in the Sunnah. It is confirmed in the Sahih that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is not a single one of you except that his companion (a devil) has been assigned to him." The Companions asked, "What about you, O Messenger of Allah?" He replied, "Yes. However, Allah has helped me against him and he has accepted Islam. Thus, he only commands me to do good." Every child of Adam has this assigned companion — the hadith's own word is *qarīnuhu*, "his companion" — who beautifies wicked deeds for him and will go to any lengths to confuse and confound him. The only person safe is the one whom Allah protects.

How close does this enemy come? It is confirmed in the Two Sahihs from Anas: Safiyyah bint Huyay came to visit the Prophet ﷺ while he was in iʿtikāf (devotional retreat in the mosque), and he went out at night to walk her back. Two men of the Ansār saw them and hurried past, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Slow down! This is Safiyyah bint Huyay!" They exclaimed, "Glory be to Allah, O Messenger of Allah!" — and he said: "Verily, Shayṭān runs in the Son of Adam like the running of the blood. And verily, I feared that he might cast something into your hearts — or he said — evil." The devil moves through a person as unnoticed as his own bloodstream — so real is the danger that even the sight of the Prophet ﷺ walking with his own wife could have become an occasion for it, which is why he clarified the matter at once. Maʿārif draws the practical lesson: just as one must avoid evil deeds, a Muslim should avoid situations that give others occasion for ill thoughts — and if such a situation arises, clarify it then and there, as the Prophet ﷺ did.

Ayah 5 names the arena: he whispers *fī ṣudūr al-nās* — into the breasts of mankind.

## "From among jinn and mankind"

Ayah 6 delivers the sūrah's final disclosure, and Ibn Kathir records two ways of reading it.

On one view, "the breasts of *al-nās*" in ayah 5 includes both mankind and jinn — for the jinn are sometimes included in the usage of the word. Ibn Jarir argued that since the Qurʼān speaks of "men from the jinn" (72:6), it is not strange for *al-nās* to be applied to them also; on this reading ayah 6 spells out that the whisperer attacks both kinds of victim.

On the other view — which Maʿārif adopts as the explanation of the verse — ayah 6 identifies two kinds of *whisperer*: the devils of the jinn and the devils of mankind both whisper into human breasts. Ibn Kathir compares Allah's saying: "And so We have appointed for every Prophet enemies — Shayāṭīn among mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with adorned speech as a delusion" (6:112).

But how can a *human* whisper, when humans come forward publicly and use their voices? Maʿārif answers: human beings too often cast doubts in the minds of people in an indirect way, without uttering them explicitly. And Shaikh ʿIzzuddin Ibn ʿAbdus-Salam, in his monograph *al-Fawāʼid fī Mushkilāt-il-Qurʼān*, held that the "whisperer from mankind" refers to the whispering of one's own *nafs* — the base self — which urges a person to evil just as Shayṭān casts evil thoughts into the mind. That is why the Messenger of Allah ﷺ directed us to pray: "O Allah! I seek asylum in You from the evil of myself, from the evil of the Shayṭān and from the evil of idolatry."

## Two enemies, two weapons

Maʿārif, drawing on Ibn Kathir's preface, notes that the Qurʼān prescribes opposite tactics for human and shaytanic enemies — and cites three passages, each in two parts (7:199–200; 23:96–98; 41:34–36). Against the human enemy: forbearance, kindness, repelling evil with what is better — "and you will see that the one you had mutual enmity with will turn as if he were a close friend" (41:34). Human nature was created uncorrupted, so goodness can win a human enemy over (and where humans become hardened aggressors, other verses prescribe resistance). But the Shayṭān is evil in his primal nature: kindness does not reform him, and armed conflict with an invisible enemy is impossible. So each passage's second half gives the only weapon that works: "And if you are stricken with a strike from the Shayṭān, seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing" (7:200). The believer's defence is *dhikr* (remembrance of Allah) and *taʿawwudh* (seeking refuge with Him) — and note that against a human enemy the believer never truly loses, for even defeat brings martyrdom's reward, whereas defeat before Shayṭān ruins the Hereafter itself. Hence refuge in Allah is the one indispensable weapon.

## The whisper is not the fall

Two consolations close the picture. First, from the Sunnah: Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah! Sometimes I say things to myself that I would rather fall from the sky than say aloud." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah is Most Great! Allah is Most Great! All praise is due to Allah Who sent his (Shayṭān's) plot back as only a whisper." Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i also recorded this hadith.

Maʿārif makes a related point as a ruling: evil thoughts are of two types, voluntary and involuntary. The sūrah warns against the voluntary — thoughts one entertains by choice. Involuntary thoughts that arrive unbidden and pass away are neither harmful nor sinful, so long as one does not act on them or speak of them.

And the enemy himself is weaker than he seems. Allah says: "No doubt, the guile of the Shayṭān is feeble" (4:76), and: "He is such that he has no power over those who believe in Allah and place trust in their Lord. His power is only over those who befriend him and those who associate partners with Him" (16:98–100). His entire arsenal is a whisper — and remembrance of Allah makes him flee.

## The Qurʼān's last word

Maʿārif ends with a beautiful observation about the Book as a whole. The Qurʼān opens with al-Fātiḥah — Allah's name, His lordship and mercy, and the prayer for guidance along the straight path. Everything man needs for success in both worlds is set out there. But on the road to that success stands the accursed Shayṭān, laying inconspicuous traps at every weak point. So the Qurʼān most fittingly ends where the seeker's journey daily begins again: with refuge in Allah — Lord, King and Ilāh of mankind — from every whisperer that would pull the heart away from Him.
